extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent lawyers, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing patent infringement: tests for when a defendant's device or process infringes a patentee's rights (mechanical equivalents, substantial identity, process vs manufacture, application of principles, and when independent invention defeats infringement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Look to the substance not to the form
rubrics_metrics.description: "you ought to look always to the substance, and not to the form."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether similarities are merely apparent (form) or whether the defendant has adopted the same principle or substance of the invention. Example: a model at first sight appeared identical until a material difference in principle was pointed out; that difference meant no similarity in principle and therefore no infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: If the change introduced by the defendant constitutes a mechanical equivalent, in reference to the means used by the patentee, it is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the defendant's change accomplishes some other advantage beyond the patentee's effect (and that advantage might itself be patentable as an improvement), the defendant still infringes as to what is covered by the patentee's patent. Illustrated by cases where a spring in a bolt was held to be the same thing as a bolt sliding in a groove, producing infringement despite differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in form does not avoid infringement if principle is same
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in form or in immaterial circumstances do not permit escape from infringement if, in reality and in substance, the defendant has availed himself of the invention of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the defendant has taken the same plan and applied it to the same purpose, varying only in process or unimportant particulars, the manufacture will be substantially identical. Example: Walton v. Potter — jury found defendants' plan in substance the same as plaintiff's despite differences in how India rubber was applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture vs process — identity of article vs process proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter of the patent is a manufacture, identity of the manufactured article may establish infringement; where the patent is for a process, infringement must be proved as to the process used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity in appearance and structure is presumptive evidence that the same process was used, but if the patent covers a process (not the article itself), the plaintiff must show the defendant used that process. If the subject is the manufacture, it is immaterial by what process it was produced — making the same thing can be infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on the plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof is always on the plaintiff to show that his process has been infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of direct evidence, identity of effect and similarity of apparatus will generally be sufficient for a jury to infer use of the same process; but the plaintiff must persuade the factfinder. Examples include Hall v. Boot and Huddart v. Grimshaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of structure as presumptive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of structure of two things is presumptive evidence of their being made in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Ellenborough's rule: where only similarity of the articles is shown, the inference that the same process was used must be drawn from the evidence; the strength of this presumption depends on whether the article could plausibly be produced by other independent processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When patent covers an application of a principle, test substantial identity of principle and its application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the real subject covered by the patent is the application of a principle in the arts or manufactures, the question on infringement is as to the substantial identity of the principle and of the application of the principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means, machinery, forms, or modifications are material only insofar as they affect the identity of the application. Examples: Forsyth (use of detonating powder as priming) and Clegg (measuring gas by alternate filling/discharging) — different apparatus may still infringe if the same application of the principle is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for a mode of carrying a principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has invented some mode of carrying a principle into effect, he is entitled to protect himself from all other modes of making the same application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant's mode shows only that the principle admits of the same application in a variety of forms or apparatus, the jury may treat that mode as a piracy of the original invention. Conversely, if the variation shows the application of the principle is varied (another law or rule of science replaces the patentee's essence), there is no infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent substantive invention defeats infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant (without borrowing from the prior patent) has invented a new mode of accomplishing the same object, he may be entitled to a patent for that discovery and not be an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that the defendant is entitled to a patent for a substantive invention is a test: he cannot have a patent unless he invented something material and new that goes to the essence and substance of the subject-matter. Example: case comparing plaintiff's caoutchouc-slice method with defendant's impregnated fabric — jury asked whether defendants added anything material not covered by plaintiff's patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements do not excuse infringement absent substantial difference in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's improvement upon a patented invention does not prevent that defendant from infringing the original patent unless there is a substantial difference in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law discriminates and rewards both discoveries: each gets exclusive property in their discovery but neither may use the other's invention without license. Example: Read's friction roller might be an improvement on Perkins's toggle-joint; nevertheless, using Perkins's principal machine without license remains infringement if principles are the same.
